channel.title: Aggregated External AI & Tech News
channel.description: Merged headlines from configured external sources

item.title: Sixteen Claude AI agents working together created a new C compiler (Source: feeds.arstechnica.com)
item.description: The $20,000 experiment compiled a Linux kernel but needed deep human management.

item.title: OpenAI researcher quits over ChatGPT ads, warns of "Facebook" path (Source: feeds.arstechnica.com)
item.description: Zoë Hitzig resigned on the same day OpenAI began testing ads in its chatbot.

item.title: Once-hobbled Lumma Stealer is back with lures that are hard to resist (Source: feeds.arstechnica.com)
item.description: ClickFix bait, combined with advanced Castleloader malware, is installing Lumma "at scale."

item.title: Attackers prompted Gemini over 100,000 times while trying to clone it, Google says (Source: feeds.arstechnica.com)
item.description: Distillation technique lets copycats mimic Gemini at a fraction of the development cost.

item.title: OpenAI sidesteps Nvidia with unusually fast coding model on plate-sized chips (Source: feeds.arstechnica.com)
item.description: OpenAI's new GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark is 15 times faster at coding than its predecessor.

item.title: Retraction: After a routine code rejection, an AI agent published a hit piece on someone by name (Source: feeds.arstechnica.com)
item.description: This story has been retracted

item.title: Most VMware users still "actively reducing their VMware footprint," survey finds (Source: feeds.arstechnica.com)
item.description: Broadcom's "strategy was never to keep every customer," CloudBolt report says.

item.title: Password managers' promise that they can't see your vaults isn't always true (Source: feeds.arstechnica.com)
item.description: Contrary to what password managers say, a server compromise can mean game over.

item.title: New AirSnitch attack bypasses Wi-Fi encryption in homes, offices, and enterprises (Source: feeds.arstechnica.com)
item.description: That guest network you set up for your neighbors may not be as secure as you think.

item.title: Google quantum-proofs HTTPS by squeezing 15kB of data into 700-byte space (Source: feeds.arstechnica.com)
item.description: Merkle Tree Certificate support is already in Chrome. Soon, it will be everywhere.

item.title: LLMs can unmask pseudonymous users at scale with surprising accuracy (Source: feeds.arstechnica.com)
item.description: Pseudonymity has never been perfect for preserving privacy. Soon it may be pointless.

item.title: Downdetector, Speedtest sold to IT service-provider Accenture in $1.2B deal (Source: feeds.arstechnica.com)
item.description: Accenture plans to buy Ookla, which also includes RootMetrics and Ekahau.

item.title: Trump gets data center companies to pledge to pay for power generation (Source: feeds.arstechnica.com)
item.description: With no enforcement and questionable economics, it may not make a difference.

item.title: Amazon appears to be down, with over 20,000 reported problems (Source: feeds.arstechnica.com)
item.description: Problems viewing products and checking out.

item.title: Feds take notice of iOS vulnerabilities exploited under mysterious circumstances (Source: feeds.arstechnica.com)
item.description: The long, strange trip of a large assembly of advanced iOS exploits.

item.title: 14,000 routers are infected by malware that's highly resistant to takedowns (Source: feeds.arstechnica.com)
item.description: Most of the devices are made by Asus and are located in the US.

item.title: The who, what, and why of the attack that has shut down Stryker's Windows network (Source: feeds.arstechnica.com)
item.description: Company says it doesn't know how long it will take to restore its Microsoft environment.

item.title: Supply-chain attack using invisible code hits GitHub and other repositories (Source: feeds.arstechnica.com)
item.description: Unicode that's invisible to the human eye was largely abandoned-until attackers took notice.

item.title: Researchers disclose vulnerabilities in IP KVMs from four manufacturers (Source: feeds.arstechnica.com)
item.description: Internet-exposed devices that give BIOS-level access? What could possibly go wrong?

item.title: Federal cyber experts called Microsoft's cloud a "pile of shit," approved it anyway (Source: feeds.arstechnica.com)
item.description: One Microsoft product was approved despite years of concerns about its security.
